articles.title: A rubber-stamp parliament
articles.content: IN a democracy, parliament is not only supposed to legislate; it is also expected to safeguard the national interest and deliberate on key policy matters. That criterion does not seem to apply to our parliament. One seldom witnesses a major foreign or national security issue being deliberated by the ‘representatives’ of the people, and there is hardly any meaningful debate even on critical constitutional amendments and legislation. This ineffectiveness of the country’s highest legislative body reflects the sorry state of democracy against the backdrop of creeping authoritarianism. Last week, both Houses of parliament approved, within hours and by a two-thirds majority, the decision to remove an elected provincial government and impose astate of emergency and governor’s rule, with no substantive debate. A highly controversial matter was disposed of within hours, with some ministers and leaders of the ruling coalition justifying the action against a provincial government that enjoyed the support of a majority of the members of the assembly, and the arrest of its chief minister and members of his government. It was obvious that the decision had already been taken elsewhere, and that a parliament of debatable legitimacy was, as usual, expected to rubber-stamp it. Most members may not even have understood the constitutional provisions invoked to declare a state of emergency in a province, or whether those provisions applied to the conditions at hand. It looked like a puppet show. But it was not the first time this parliament blindly toed the line. Over the past two years, it has passed the26thand27th Amendments, virtually destroying the essence of a Constitution that rests on the independence of the judiciary. That was perhaps the most shameful moment in our parliamentary history: ministers were shown the draft only hours before the session, and members were handed it on the floor of the House. Most had not read it when they voted for amendments of critical importance. They were passed overnight. One can hardly recollect a foreign or national security policy being debated in parliament, nor even in its committees; one wonders whether such policies are discussed and approved by the cabinet at all. The main reason the government has given for its action in KP is that the provincial government was unwilling to cooperate in counterterrorism operations in the province worst hit by the resurgence of militant violence. The ruling coalition is bound to pay a heavy political price for its undemocratic actions. But a question that is never answered is whether the state has a well-defined, overarching counterterrorism policy in place, and, if it does, whether that policy has ever been discussed in cabinet, let alone presented before parliament or any of its committees for deliberation. The truth is that we have no clarity on how to deal with this existential threat. Over the past quarter of a century I have covered and written extensively on Pakistan’s struggle with terrorism, and I can vouch that we have never had a holistic approach to an issue for which the state itself has been responsible. Even now, as militant attacks claim the lives of an increasing number of security personnel, the state is pursuing a one-dimensional policy that relies solely on kinetic operations in the affected areas, with little success. The confusion persists despite the claims of the ‘hard state’. Balochistan, another strategically located province, has been bleeding for over 25 years with rising separatist militancy. As a result, the state has now lost control of large parts of the province, with an unrepresentative provincial government at the helm. Yet neither the cabinet nor parliament has any say in such a grave national security matter. While the ousted provincial government is being held responsible for the worsening situation in KP, who is responsible for the state of affairs in Balochistan? The reality is that the policy on Balochistan lies outside the domain of the present civilian set-up or the so-called representative parliament. Unsurprisingly, a critical foreign policy question — Pakistan’s signing of the trilateralMakkah Joint Defence Agreement— has not been ratified, or more precisely rubber-stamped, by parliament. Turkiye, the other signatory to the pact, is still waiting for its parliament to endorse it. It is an extremely important external and internal policy issue, with long-term implications for a country already facing multiple challenges. There is also the question of whether the pact will be activated with the escalation in the Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia. While a pliant parliament has been conveniently used to rubber-stamp controversial constitutional amendments and laws that curb judicial independence and freedom of expression, there has also been much talk about resetting the country’s administrative structure. The all-powerful and ubiquitous interior minister has publicly declared that the system has collapsed and called for a complete revamp. But what does this projected resetting mean for the present hybrid power structure and for parliament? There are strong views that emergency rule in KP could be the first step towards extending it to the entire country. Will a parliament that has endorsed emergency rule in KP also rubber-stamp any such action, even though it would further curtail its own powers? One objective of emergency rule is to clear the ground for the resetting of administrative units, an extremely volatile issue for some of the coalition parties, particularly the PPP. The Sindh Assembly has already voted against administrative changes. Still, with the legitimacy question hanging over its head, it would be extremely hard for parliament to resist a measure that would further consolidate authoritarian rule in the country. The ruling coalition — which has feverishly supported emergency rule in KP, the controversial constitutional amendments that curb judicial independence, and the Peca laws being deployed to control the media — will pay a heavy political price for its undemocratic actions that are paving the way for the winding up of the entire system. The shadow of authoritarianism looms over the country as a parliament with a dubious mandate has already surrendered whatever little power it had left. The collapse of a system built on a mandate seen as stolen seems imminent, with its patrons planning a new setup. It will be a further leap backward, taking an already unstable state down a dangerous path.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: The generational bargain
articles.content: OVER my working life, I have watched the next generation enter organisations with different expectations. Business leaders today frequently complain that younger employees view careers, loyalty and work differently from earlier generations. That may be so, but we should also ask whether the economic proposition attached to work has changed. For many young people today, the connection between work, progress and economic security is much less certain. Perhaps that is one reason something interesting is happening across very different parts of the world. In France, Spain, Belgium, and Albania, young people have been prominent in protests around issues pertaining to education, housing, public services, living costs, and austerity. In India, a youth-led protest movement that began around examinations and electoral processes appears to reflect a deeper frustration about jobs, opportunity and institutions. The circumstances are clearly different, and it would be simplistic to describe this as a single global movement. But perhaps young people in these very different societies are asking versions of the same question. Does the economic system they have inherited still offer them a credible path towards a better life? For much of the post-World War II period, the bargain was reasonably clear. Get educated, find employment, work hard, buy a home, accumulate some assets, and eventually retire with reasonable security. Each generation could expect to live better than the previous one. But this bargain is beginning to look less certain. When we think about inequality, we normally think about rich and poor, or capital and labour. An important divide nowadays may, instead, be between those who already own assets and those still trying to acquire them. Property, financial assets, pensions, family businesses, and inherited wealth all create advantages that compound over time. The child of a family that already owns capital begins adult life in a fundamentally different position from someone who depends entirely on wages. This does not mean that wealth accumulated legitimately is wrong. Saving, investment, entrepreneurship, and risk-taking remain essential to economic progress. The more difficult question is what happens when advantage becomes self-perpetuating. Across very different societies, young people are asking whether the economic system still offers them a credible stake in the future. Europe faces another dimension of this problem. Young workers are entering economies with expensive housing, strained public services, and ageing populations. At the same time, they are being asked to finance pension and welfare systems created under very different demographic conditions. The current protests across Europe differ in their immediate causes, but education, housing, public services, and living costs repeatedly appear among the grievances. India presents almost the opposite demographic picture, yet the underlying anxiety can be surprisingly similar. Its economy has continued to grow rapidly, but growth alone does not guarantee the quantity and quality of employment expected by an increasingly educated young population. Recent protests have had specific institutional triggers, but concern about opportunity and the credibility of the pathway from education to employment sits in the background. How are young people everywhere reacting to the underlying issues? Some respond by demanding greater redistribution and stronger public services. Others move towards nationalist or populist politics. Others simply lose confidence in established institutions. Governments often point to achievements in economic growth, employment or falling inflation and struggle to understand why dissatisfaction remains so intense. But young people may be asking a different question. They are not simply asking whether the economy is growing. They are asking whether they can build a secure life within it. This may also explain why younger employees sometimes seem less attached to careers and organisations than earlier generations were. A young person may have a respectable income but still be unable to buy a home, accumulate meaningful assets, or feel confident about retirement. Economically, such a person may be classified as middle class. In lived experience, they may feel permanently insecure. An emerging divide, therefore, may not simply be between the rich and poor. It is between those who already possess economic security and those still trying to acquire it. That is a more difficult problem for governments, because it cannot be solved simply by increasing GDP. This is where Pakistan should pay attention. We always describe our young population as a demographic dividend. But demographics do not create dividends by themselves. Young people become an economic asset only when an economy can educate them, employ them productively, and give them a reasonable expectation that effort will improve their lives. What exactly is the bargain we offer a young Pakistani today? Get educated, compete for too few productive jobs, struggle with housing and asset prices that have moved well beyond ordinary incomes, enter an economy in which family capital and connections matter enormously, and help support a state carrying large pension and debt obligations accumulated over previous decades. Economic systems ultimately require legitimacy. People are more willing to accept unequal outcomes when they believe opportunity remains open, effort is rewarded, and their children have a reasonable prospect of advancement. Once that confidence disappears, inequality becomes more than a statistic. It becomes political. For much of the past century, the debate around capitalism has centred on whether markets can generate growth and prosperity. The harder question now is whether the prosperity they generate continues to offer succeeding generations a meaningful stake in it. Unless young people can see a credible route from education to work and from work to economic security, the problem will not simply be that they have less than previous generations. It will be that they no longer believe the system gives them a fair chance. And that is what the protests everywhere are beginning to tell us and what business leaders and policymakers at home need to pay attention to. The writer advises boards and CEOs on strategy, leadership and organisational transformation.
articles.author: Asif Saad

articles.title: Season of uprisings
articles.content: PERHAPS the most unfortunate aspect of the latest French popular uprising is that it may well facilitate Marine Le Pen’s journey to the Élysée Palace. The far-right contender for the presidency poses as the law-and-order saviour for a France that no longer exists, focusing — like the Trump regime — on immigration as the source of every societal woe. The unrest that erupted in September with students from a couple of public high schools complaining about shrinking resources and inadequate facilities ballooned into a much broader rebellion. By last weekend, theprotestshad extended beyond disenchanted pupils and their parents and teachers to a far wider cross-section of society complaining about the cost of living — alongside the usual panoply of vandals, looters, and arsonists. The latter were on the fringes of largely peaceful demonstrations but inevitably grabbed the headlines, featuring images of shattered shopfronts and the historic Limoges town hall in flames. To be fair, though, almost every report I came across acknowledged the carnivalesque aspect of the huge marches, distinguishing it from the criminality of opportunist gangs. Even President Emmanuel Macron made thatdistinctionin his unimpressive address to the nation on Sunday, but offered little more than retribution for the offenders and a dialogue with ‘stakeholders’. Earlier, in response to the students’ demands, the government promised 3,000 more substitute teachers, but that’s not likely to alleviate concerns. With France’s national debt at 119pc of its GDP, the usual excuse is that the state cannot afford to throw money at education (or health), let alone consider social spending that might ease wider cost-of-living woes. Yet economists have worked out that a relatively small increase in inheritance tax for the wealthiest one per cent of heirs would suffice for a substantial investment in education, while Thomas Piketty notes that the growth in private wealth means “France has never been richer”, notwithstanding its public debt. Echoes of 1968 have been discerned in the events in France. That’s a familiar story. In Europe alone, economic woes have prompted mass protests from the Iberian Peninsula to Albania. The rough end of the European housing crisis featured prominently in Spain, where citizens revolted once more after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly evicted from her home of 70 years because she could not afford the 230pc rent increase. She died a fortnight later, prompting more outrage. A snap election has been called for Nov 29 after the right-wing opposition thwarted two decrees from the Pedro Sánchez government aimed at redressing tenants’ woes. Similar concerns have brought Portuguese citizens to the streets, and broader affordability worries have led to protests in Belgium and Italy. In Albania, meanwhile, the‘flamingo’ proteststhat grew from environmental concerns over an island that Donald Trump’s daughter and son-in-law sought to colonise have expanded to include less esoteric concerns, spreading from the capital Tirana to various other cities and demanding the departure of the prime minister and opposition leader. La France Insoumise, the only viable left-wing force in French politics, has backed the agitators and condemned the violence, but should LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon make it into the second round of the next presidential election, there’s little doubt that the extreme centre epitomised by Macron will opt for Le Pen, effectively authorising a second Vichy regime. Similar patterns are likely to be witnessed in the rest of the continent. Happily, the prospects in India differ. There is no scope for complacency, but theCockroach Janta Partyand its allies have clearly rattled the Modi regime. Its demise may not be imminent, but it’s no longer inconceivable. Every country deserves a Neha Bora. Several commentators in Pakistan have lamented the lack of parallels. Sorrow and angst were expressed after 34 pupils and a teacher were killed last week in aroof collapse at a private Peshawar school.In many other countries, such a tragedy would have prompted demands for a nationwide reckoning, not least because of the criminally low state spending on education. But Pakistan, it seems, has better things to do. Echoes of 1968 have been discerned in the events in France. Back then, university students, eventually backed by the unionised working class, briefly chased away Charles de Gaulle. He returned in apparent triumph but was gone within a year. Meanwhile, our first field marshal, hailed by his Western sponsors as Pakistan’s de Gaulle, departed for good after a student-led popular rebellion in 1968-69. It isn’t necessary to condone what followed to hail the demise of the Ayub regime as a tremendous achievement. But perhaps it’s also a reminder to be careful what you wish for, given what followed in the next decade.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: Drainage disaster
articles.content: DRAINAGE and the ultimate disposal of agricultural effluent are complex problems. Sindh has faced the catastrophic consequences of flawed design and substandard execution of mega drainage projects — mainly the Left Bank Outfall Drain and the Right Bank Outfall Drain. Wapda has designed, executed, and monitored these poorly conceived projects. The LBOD system has become a flooding menace in the districts of lower Sindh, while the RBOD has devastated the once-pristine Manchhar Lake. At the tail end of the Indus Basin Irrigation System, Sindh is unfairly seen as a sink for effluent from the basin’s irrigation network. The World Bank-financed National Drainage Programme, initiated in 1997, proposed a national surface drainage system to transport the Indus Basin Irrigation System’s saline effluent to the sea, using Sindh as a conduit. This prescription collapsed when the multi-donor-funded LBOD project failed miserably to handle the agricultural effluent of just three districts. A critical component of the Cholri weir on the drain suffered severe scouring soon after becoming operational and eventually collapsed. This debacle forced proponents of the national surface drainage system to retreat from the scheme, as ultimate disposal into the sea became a nightmare. Since then, the LBOD is seen as a blot on Wapda’s engineering credentials. The RBOD experience proved worse, as the project inflicted an ecological disaster on Manchhar Lake, once Pakistan’s largest freshwater body. Wapda’s design allowed drainage effluent to flow from the right-bank districts into Manchhar Lake. Within a few years, this drain devastated the lake by turning it into a vast pond of effluent. Hundreds of self-sufficient families living on the bank or nearby lost their livelihoods in fishing and agriculture. The disaster compelled them to migrate from the area. Wapda’s serious lack of capacity to design, execute, and manage mega drainage projects thus stood exposed. Despite this history of failure, Wapda has proposed another scheme — the Ghotki drainage project — as a solution to waterlogging and salinity in the area. The proposed project is estimated to cost a whopping Rs156.217 billion and would cover the construction of a 1,067-kilometre drainage network across Ubauro, Daharki, Khangarh, and Mirpur Mathelo in Ghotki District. Four drainage systems — the Karo Naro, Raitee, Rainee, and Thar — will carry an effluent discharge of 3,183 cusecs. Clearly, no lessons have been learnt from the Manchhar disaster. The project proposes two major outfalls into the Nara Canal. No lessons have been learned from the Manchhar Lake fiasco. The project’s environmental and social impact assessment recognises that unplanned disposal of such water will create environmental issues in other areas and at disposal sites. However, surprisingly, the assessment provides no data on dilution. It also does not mention the expected impact on the water quality of Nara Canal when a substantial quantity of saline effluent is discharged during the low-flow season. This serious omission raises concerns about the quality and credibility of the ESIA. Nara is Sindh’s longest irrigation canal. It passes through Khairpur, Sanghar, Mirpurkhas, Umerkot, and Tharparkar, irrigating 2.2 million acres of land. According to the Sindh Irrigation and Drainage Authority, the canal is the primary source of freshwater for irrigation, drinking, and domestic use for a population of 6.6m, which is served by 127 drinking-water schemes, along with numerous authorised and unauthorised connections. Releasing large quantities of untreated effluent can pollute canal water to harmful levels, potentially causing a public health disaster, especially during low flows. Moreover, the proposed effluent disposal mechanism violates the recommendations of a commission of inquiry constituted by the Supreme Court in 2016. The commission advised against disposing of untreated wastewater into irrigation canals. Although the project scope does not explicitly mention extending the drain to the neighbouring district of Rahim Yar Khan in Punjab, the possibility cannot be ruled out once the new drain is operational. Under the Salinity Control and Reclamation Project, an unquantified volume of effluent from Rahim Yar Khan is presently being discharged in the desert of the dehs of Poh and Sutiaro in Ghotki. A vast area remains inundated by drainage effluent and has been rendered infertile due to unabated effluent flows from Punjab into Ghotki. Drainage projects have already wreaked havoc in Sindh. The province cannot afford a new ecological menace.
articles.author: Naseer Memon

articles.title: Real FBR reform
articles.content: REFORM of the FBR has always been easier to promise than to deliver. Since the late 1990s, governments have tried restructuring, automation, and compliance drives. However, the institution has resisted every change that threatens the entrenched interests within. The basic weaknesses remain a narrow tax base, widespread evasion, and an administration whose discretionary powers invite corruption. Greater transparency, independent oversight, and reduced contact with taxpayers all threaten arrangements from which officials benefit. That helps explain why change keeps meeting opposition from within the organisation. The recent pen-down strike call by Inland Revenue officers against the reforms showed that this was no ordinary bureaucratic disagreement. Lost revenue is only a part of the cost of business-as-usual at the FBR. Taxpayers deal directly with officials enjoying wide discretion, which opens the door to harassment and bribery. Businesses and individuals spend time and money on assessments, audits, and disputes, with some paying to avoid trouble even if they have complied. Others stay outside the net because they fear registration will bring arbitrary demands and prolonged dealings with tax officials. Such an administration makes compliance costly and unpredictable, which discourages voluntary registration, erodes trust, and penalises those who already pay. Influential evaders exploit loopholes, while compliant businesses carry the burden. A fairer system cannot be built by squeezing the same documented taxpayers, while much of the potential base stays out of reach. The proposed faceless assessment and audit system reduces contact between officials and taxpayers, centralises assessments, and relies on third-party data, which narrows room for discretionary abuse and tries to build public trust in the system. But digitisation alone will not end corruption. Systems can be exploited unless audit selection is transparent and decisions are traceable. Taxpayers need an effective appeals route, and officials who abuse their powers must face real penalties. Independent oversight is equally important. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s recent warning that resistance to the ongoing reforms will not be tolerated is, therefore, welcome. But unless his government confronts the forces that frustrated earlier attempts, this one may go the way of previous efforts to stem the rot. He is right that reform must continue despite the resistance. Better salaries and official facilities should be tied to integrity and performance. Disciplinary action against individual officers, however necessary, is no substitute for changing the incentives and structures that allow corruption to persist. Reform should be judged by whether the tax base widens, compliance gets easier, and taxpayers are treated fairly. The country cannot afford another round in which resistance is briefly overcome, old arrangements return after a few months, and honest taxpayers pay for the failure.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Missing lawmakers
articles.content: FOLLOWING theimpositionof emergency and governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11, many lawmakers of the PTI remain untraceable. The matter has been raised in parliament and in the courts. During a hearing of related petitions in the Peshawar High Court yesterday, PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan said that 12 MNAs and 14 MPAs belonging to the KP Assembly had been “picked up”. Soon after the proclamation of emergency, Federal Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry had confirmed that KP’s non-functional Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and some members of his cabinet were in “preventive custody”. Meanwhile, on Monday, PTI lawmakers in the National Assembly demanded production orders for their fellow party MNAs. Opposition Leader Mahmood Achakzai endorsed the demand, while Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, raised the issue in the Upper House. One PTI MNA has beenarrestedat his madressah in Bannu, but the whereabouts of most of the missing lawmakers remain unknown, with their families also in the dark. Some lawmakers have reportedly been in detention since before Oct 11. This is not the first time that opposition lawmakers in Pakistan have gone ‘missing’. The proclamation of emergency should not, however, mean holding fundamental rights in abeyance. Whether it is members of the assemblies, or ordinary citizens, the Constitution — if that document still holds any value for the wielders of power — guarantees due process to every Pakistani. Therefore, Mr Afridi, as well as other PTI lawmakers, must be produced before the courts forthwith. The state must announce publicly what they are accused of, so that they can defend themselves, and engage counsel of their choice. Mr Chaudhry had said that if there are cases against the PTI leaders they would be charged, and if no evidence is found against them they would be released. The state must keep its promise, and also grant the lawmakers access to their families. Members of the ruling coalition — belonging to both the PML-N and PPP — were on the receiving end of the state’s excesses during their time in opposition. Perhaps they should remember their own experiences, and the commitments their leaders made to upholding the rule of law.
articles.author: Editorial
